title: TB0-17470
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXXXXX, is a citizen of Turkey who seeks refugee protection pursuant to subsections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 Allegations

The complete story alleging the basis of the claimant's fear is captured in the Personal Information Form (PIF).2 The claimant alleges that he fears returning to Turkey due to his involvement with Alevi-Kurdish leftist activities where he was detained, beaten and tortured four separate times. The claimant also objects in serving in the Turkish military due to the human rights violations of the military that he believes he will be required to commit against Kurds like himself. The claimant departed Turkey on XXXX, 2008 for the United States and arrived illegally in Canada at Vancouver on XXXXXXX, 2010 and filed a refugee claim on November 15, 2010. Decision

The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The panel also finds that should the claimant return to Turkey he would not be subjected personally to a risk to his life or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. Further, on substantial grounds there is no danger of torture. Identity
On a balance of probabilities, the panel is willing to accept that the claimant is a citizen of Turkey based on copies of his passport as seen in exhibit R/A-2. Analysis

The determinative issue in this case is the credibility of the evidence as submitted. On the issue of credibility, the panel is guided by the Federal Court of Appeal case in Sellan3 which stated the following: Where the Board makes a general finding that the claimant lacks credibility, that determination is sufficient to dispose of the claim unless there is independent and credible documentary evidence in the record capable of supporting a positive disposition of the claim. The claimant bears the onus of demonstrating there was such evidence.

Furthermore, the Federal Court notes the following: The Board is in a much better position than a reviewing court to gage the credibility and plausibility of a refugee claimant's story. A credibility finding is not a finding of mixed fact and law. It is a finding of fact, pure and simple. Findings of fact made by the Board may only be interfered with by a reviewing court if the finding was made in a perverse or capricious manner or without regard for the material before it (see the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, paragraph 18.1(4)(d)). Indeed, it was Parliament's express intention that administrative fact finding would command this high degree of deference (see Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa, 2009 SCC 12, [2009] S.C.J. No. 12 (QL) at paragraph 46). Thus, credibility findings of the Board are to be reviewed against the statutory standard of review provided for in paragraph 18.1(4)(d) of the Federal Courts Act (see Diabo v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 1772, [2004] F.C.J. No. 2168 (QL) at paragraph 3).

The panel noted that the claimant's alleged activities with a human rights group, SIVAS, and his membership with SDP and Alevi associations was because he believed in the cause for Kurds and seeking their human rights. The claimant stated that the SDP and Alevi associations were aware of his activities which resulted in him being detained, beaten and tortured by the authorities in four separate occasions. The claimant was asked if he had any corroborating evidence from the alleged groups he was somehow involved with which could possibly credibly support his problems; he responded in the negative.

The panel does recognize there is a brief letter from XXXXXXXXXX Cultural Association, as seen in Exhibit C-9, indicating the claimant's membership from the years 2005 to 2010. However, the letter provides no information as to the level of the claimant's activities and problems as alleged by the claimant from the authorities. The panel does not find it would be such an unreasonable expectation for the claimant to have provided satisfactory corroborating evidence from the SDP or Alevi groups in Turkey that the claimant alleges membership or affiliation with regarding his problems from the authorities, given they were aware of his problems from the authorities. The panel makes a negative credibility finding for the lack of corroborating evidence pertaining to his alleged problems in Turkey.

The panel does recognize that in support of the claimant's problems, he submitted an Affidavit from his cousin, which was sworn on XXXXX, 2012. The Affidavit was submitted to attest to the claimant's activities and problems from authorities. The panel gives little weight to the Affidavit from the claimant's cousin as the information obtained pertaining to the claimant's alleged situation in Turkey is second hand. The deponent, the claimant's cousin, was not in Turkey when the alleged problems of the claimant occurred. The deponent left Turkey in 1995 for the United States and came to Canada in XXXXX 2008. Therefore, the information by the deponent was obtained from the claimant's mother with no supporting evidence from the claimant's mother.

Furthermore, if the claimant did have problems from the authorities as alleged and for whatever reason he could not have obtained documentation from SIVAS, SDP or Alevi groups, then there is no indication why the claimant's mother did not submit a letter detailing the claimant's problems as alleged in Turkey for the panel to review and comment, given the claimant's cousin obtained evidence from the claimant's mother pertaining to his problems in Turkey. The claimant has the burden of proving that he has a well founded fear of persecution if required to return to Turkey. Consequently, the lack of independent corroborating evidence also negatively impacts the credibility of the story as so alleged.

The panel acknowledges that the claimant has attempted to provide corroborative evidence to support his claim. However, the documents submitted inspires little confidence and lacks independent, credible information that would lead this panel to conclude that the claimant's political profile is what he wants this panel to believe and that as a consequence his life would be at risk. Also, the panel is duly concerned as to the lack of corroborating evidence from the groups and associations in Turkey the claimant was allegedly affiliated with as a member or otherwise.

The panel rejects the evidence from the claimant that the organizations would get into trouble if they describe his problems and send to the claimant. The panel has insufficient evidence to conclude that the authorities would intercept evidence submitted on behalf of the claimant which would in turn create problems for the association the claimant was allegedly involved with. The claimant is not a person of high profile or the like to create such scrutiny and interest from the authorities. This does negatively affect the believability of the story as put forward.

Credibility is a serious issue for the panel regarding the claim as put forward. On the issue of corroborating evidence, the panel wishes to note the following Federal Court case in Bhagat,4 which states the following: Corroborating evidence is not always necessary to establish the applicant's subjective fear. The Board, however, determined that in the particular circumstances of this case, corroborating evidence of persecution was expected. An absence of corroborating evidence, then, permitted it to make a negative inference against credibility of the applicant. The respondent relies on Sheik v. Canada (M.E.I.) (C.A.), [1990] 3 F.C. 238, at page 244, for its argument that the Board did not err in law when making that conclusion: The concept of "credible evidence" is not, of course, the same as that of the credibility of the applicant, but it is obvious that where the only evidence before a tribunal linking the applicant to his claim is that of the applicant himself (in addition, perhaps, to "country reports" from which nothing about the applicant's claim can be directly deduced), a tribunal's perception that he is not a credible witness effectively amounts to a finding that there is no credible evidence on which the second-level tribunal could allow his claim. In Adu v. Canada (M.E.I.), [1995] F.C.J. No. 114 (QL), the Federal Court of Appeal found that it is reasonable to expect documentary evidence of the existence of a law and stated: The "presumption" that a claimant's sworn testimony is true is always rebuttable, and, in appropriate circumstances, may be rebutted by the failure of the documentary evidence to mention what one would normally expect it to mention.

On a balance of probabilities, the panel is willing to accept that the claimant is an Alevi and Kurd but not that his life is at risk as an Alevi-Kurd, even though the panel recognizes that Alevis and Kurds, in reviewing the exhibits from counsel and the Board have and continue to experience problems in Turkey that are discriminatory and at times persecutory.

In this case as submitted, the claimant was not schooled at a school for Kurdish students nor was he subjected to inferior education due to being Kurdish. The claimant has 14 years of education and was a XXXXXXXXX from 2006 to 2008 in Turkey. Coupled with the credibility concerns as to the believability of the claimant's story, the panel has not been remotely convinced that as an Alevi-Kurd, the claimant suffered persecution as alleged or would suffer such persecution in the future if required to return to Turkey.

Furthermore, the claimant also states he cannot return to Turkey as he objects to serving in the military and due to his objection he will be punished for refusing to serve. The claimant would need to know, if required to serve in the Turkish military, who he would be fighting with. If it is Kurds like him, he would be forced to commit human rights abuses and shoot his own people.

In examining the evidence further, the panel wishes to note Exhibit C-9, pages 7-8, which is a military document issued at the request of the claimant dated May 7, 2008. The document states "the person whose identity information is stated below does not have any objection until 21.02.2011." If the claimant is a conscientious objector as he says he is, there is no credible reason why the claimant would have sought a military letter that indicates he has no objection until a later date. The panel does doubt the veracity of the evidence in relation to the claimant's alleged conscientious objection.

The panel asked the claimant whether he would join the military and fight if Turkey was invaded by a foreign nation. The claimant stated that it depends on the situation at the time and it would depend on why the foreign nation is invading Turkey. It is noted that the claimant did not say under any circumstances that he would not bear arms as a conscientious objector. However, even if the claimant had and he is truly a conscientious objector, that in of itself does not amount to persecution where a country does not have alternative service. In Turkey, as so seen in Exhibit C-5, if one refuses to serve in the military by reason of conscience, the punishment is criminal prosecution. This is a law of general application.

In Hinzman,5 the Federal Court stated the following: My conclusion in this regard is reinforced by the recent decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in Ates v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [2005] F.C.J. No. 1661. In Ates, the Court stated that even in a country where military service is compulsory and where there is no alternative to military service available, the repeated prosecutions and imprisonments of a sincere conscientious objector does not amount to persecution on a Convention ground. If persecution does not arise in the circumstances described in Ates, then surely the prosecution and potential imprisonment of a volunteer soldier by a country that does provide some, albeit limited, alternatives to military service would similarly not amount to persecution on a Convention ground.

Furthermore, the panel asked the claimant whether he made an asylum claim in the United States while in that country for two years and six months given the problems as alleged in his Personal Information Form and oral evidence. The claimant indicated that he entered the United States as a student in XXXXX and XXXXXXXX and that he did not make an asylum claim in the United States. The claimant's passport does confirm a five years multiple Visa issued on XXXX, 2008 and valid until XXXXX, 2013 for the purposes of study at XXXXX College in XXXXXX, Pennsylvania.

It should be noted that shortly after the claimant's arrival in the United States, he was charged with driving without a license, simple assault, reckless endangerment and two counts of disorderly conduct. The claimant was convicted on XXXXXX, 2009 of disorderly conduct.

The claimant stated that when he went to the United States he did not plan on claiming in the United States as he heard he could not, or it would be difficult, as the United States and Turkey are allies. The claimant also says that it was his plan to finish his studies in the United States, apply for an employment authorization, and then apply for permanent residence in the U.S.

Subjectively speaking, it was not even a mere consideration for the claimant to claim asylum in the United States given his alleged problems. If so, he would have claimed given the alleged detentions, beatings and torture he allegedly sustained by the authorities in Turkey. The claimant was in the United States for a temporary purpose and should have known that at some point he would be required to return to Turkey. Given this situation and the alleged problems as so described, which the panel does not believe took place to the point that the claimant suffered or would suffer persecution should he be required to return to Turkey, suggests clearly enough to the panel that the claimant never had it in his mind to seek asylum in the United States while there for 2.5 years. As a consequence of the lack of subjective fear, this affects negatively the objective fear.

It also must be noted that due to the claimant's criminal problems in the United States, his mind should have been turned to the fact that he will likely be required to return to Turkey. It is alleged that his U.S. lawyer told him that he would have problems obtaining a Green Card and that making an asylum claim would not be logical. The panel does not believe the claimant's evidence in this regard. If the claimant stated that he wished to claim asylum, after his criminal problems in the U.S., it makes little sense why his lawyer would say it is not logical given the story as alleged before this panel.

However, even if his U.S. lawyer did state to the claimant that it was not a logical idea to claim asylum in the U.S., the fact is, as the panel sees it, the claimant had no subjective or objective fear in the first place. The claimant chose to come to Canada and make a refugee claim on November 15, 2010 as a mere after-thought given that his life was allegedly at risk after the detention from the authorities where he was detained, beaten and tortured on XXXXX, 2008. Accordingly, the lack of action in making an asylum claim in the United States, given the 2.5 years he was there, detracts from the claimant's credibility and truthfulness of the claim as so alleged.

On the issue of not claiming in the United States, the panel notes the following Federal Court of Canada case law, Matos Quintana,6 which states: Considering the obvious lack of credibility regarding the event at the centre of the claim, it was not unreasonable to not grant any probative value to all the documents submitted by the applicant. (Satinder Pal Singh) (3) It was not unreasonable to determine that the fact that the applicant did not claim refugee status in the United States - a country where he spent three months and for which he had a five-year visa could undermine his credibility.

It should also be noted that the panel has had an opportunity to read the medical letter, as seen in Exhibit C-11 from Dr. XXXX dated XXXXX, 2012, describing the claimant's injuries which, in his opinion, after an examination, are consistent with the injuries from the police. The doctor has no idea that the injuries stem from police assaults. In fact it could be from many possibilities. While it is possible that the claimant suffered injuries from the police, the varied credibility concerns raised, as it addresses the truthfulness of the story, inspires little confidence that the claimant suffered problems and injuries as so alleged.

As stated in Rokni,7 a psychiatric letter submitted as evidence and in this case a medical letter "cannot possibly serve as a cure-all for any and all deficiencies in a claimant's testimony". The court reiterated its position in Danailov,8 with respect to the assessment of a physician's evidence and the question of the assessment of credibility; it was stated "that opinion evidence is only as valid as the truth of the facts on which it is based."

In submissions from the claimant's lawyer, it was requested for the panel to exercise its discretion and allow more time for the claimant to provide the original documents of which the panel has only seen the copies for what has already been submitted into evidence and documents from SDP. The panel advised that more time would not be given for the claimant to obtain the original documents which he believes an interpreter has or for him to provide additional documentation to prove his case. The claimant left Turkey on XXXX, 2008 and has been in Canada since XXXXXXX, 2010. There has been more than sufficient time for the claimant to have gathered all of his material, inclusive of the originals for the hearing held on March 20, 2012 with a view of meeting his onus.

Notwithstanding the panel's position regarding not providing more time for the claimant to provide original documents and other material, the panel will consider them given such information was received at the Board on March 21, 2012. In reviewing the post hearing submissions, referenced as Exhibit C-12, the panel notes for example the letter from SDP, Socialist Democratic Party is brief and contains little information that would suggest that the claimant's life was at risk or would be at risk based on the claimant's activities in Turkey. If this was so the case, then it would be reasonable to expect that the claimant would have made a claim and provide the appropriate supporting documentary evidence to U.S. immigration authorities while he was in the United States for 2.5 years. The letter from SDP does not off-set the panel's concerns regarding the well foundedness of the claim. The panel gives little weight to the letter from SDP as so submitted.

Further, the panel notes in Exhibit C-12 a membership application form from an Alevi Cultural Association dated July 15, 2007. This is a membership application and does not prove that the claimant is or was a member of the said Alevi association of the XXXXX Branch. Even if the claimant was, that does not indicate that as a member of such an organization that the claimant's life was or would be at risk because of who he is as an Alevi and what he did. The panel again gives little weight to the document.

In regards to the military document in C-12, it does not appear to be an original document from the military in Turkey. However, even if it is, it has been referred to earlier in these reasons and does not change the panel's position in this regard. The panel assigns little or no weight to this document.

Therefore, in a forward looking analysis, there is little or no credible evidence that the panel has to conclude that the evidence provided by the claimant is trustworthy enough to believe that the claimant's life is at risk based on what has been alleged. In this particular case, the panel has difficulty believing the evidence as so submitted. The panel is of the view that there is not a serious possibility or reasonable chance that the claimant would face persecution for a Convention ground if he were to return to Turkey or that his life will be at risk. The claimant would not suffer cruel or unusual treatment or punishment or on substantial grounds, there is no danger of torture should the claimant return to Turkey. Conclusion

Having considered all the evidence, the panel finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee as he has not established that there is a reasonable chance or serious possibility that he would be persecuted for a Convention ground or there would be a risk to his life or he would be subjected to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should he be required to return to Turkey. On substantial grounds, there is no danger of torture should the claimant return to Turkey. The panel rejects this claim pursuant to both sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA. (signed) "K. Dickenson" K.
